open_obligations: Note that neither odds ratio is statistically significant.
Check which group's priors are inaccurate on each claim.
Check who the participants were and whether they had any judge training; the cited passage calls them only participants, whereas Michael et al. ask for human judges to be evaluated and trained.

Note that Rahman et al. group judges by belief orientation (mainstream versus skeptical), not by strength of prior; check whether either group's priors are strong, as in Michael et al.'s open problem.
out.other_title: Does debate still work when judges hold strong inaccurate priors or cognitive biases?
out.rationale: Michael et al. call for evaluating debate where judges have strong inaccurate priors. Rahman et al. report that under consultancy mainstream-prior judges were less accurate than skeptical ones (OR 0.70, p = 0.11), while under debate accuracy was nearly identical across prior groups (OR 1.10, p = 0.66); neither odds ratio is significant.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate still works when judges hold differing prior beliefs (mainstream versus skeptical), for COVID-19 claims

text: The paper reports that under consultancy participants with mainstream prior beliefs about COVID-19 showed lower accuracy than those with skeptical prior beliefs (odds ratio 0.70, 95% CI [0.42, 1.10], p = 0.11), while debate settings showed virtually identical accuracy regardless of belief orientation (OR = 1.10, 95% CI [0.71, 1.71], p = 0.66).
title: Prior-belief effects on accuracy: consultancy vs debate odds ratios
